title: How to Spot a Fake Medical Bill in Claims and Leave Reviews
summary: How to spot a fake medical bill: who issues a bill, statement and EOB, how to use NPPES and CMS code sets, and how to confirm with the provider.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** A fake medical bill is a billing document that was edited after a provider issued it, or generated for care that never occurred. The Justice Department's 2026 National Health Care Fraud Takedown charged 455 defendants over more than $6.5 billion in alleged false claims, a figure about provider-side schemes and not a rate for forged bills. A real NPI and valid codes do not prove treatment happened, so the deciding step is confirming the account with the provider through a channel the reviewer found independently.


## What a Real Bill, Statement, and EOB Are


Three documents get called a medical bill, and they come from different issuers. Who should have produced the page is the first test.


A medical bill comes from the provider or facility billing office.[CMS's guide to reading a medical bill](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/how-read-your-bill) lists what patients are likely to see: the patient's name and address, a statement date, the provider or facility, an account number assigned by that provider, dates of service, descriptions of services or supplies, charges, adjustments, insurance and patient payments, the balance due, and how to pay. Real bills vary in layout and detail.


An itemized statement also comes from the provider or facility. It breaks a summary balance into individual services, and the CFPB notes it is sometimes called a superbill, showing each procedure code, what insurance paid, and what the patient owes. A summary bill without codes is normal, so request the itemized version before reading anything into missing detail.


An Explanation of Benefits comes from the health plan. CMS is direct that an EOB is not a bill. It shows the services, the dates, what the plan agrees to pay, and what the patient may owe. A page presented as an EOB that carries a provider's letterhead and a pay-now coupon has the wrong issuer. CMS also says patients should generally receive the EOB before the provider's bill, apart from copayments or coinsurance collected at the visit.


Document Issued by What it establishes What it does not establish


Medical bill Provider or facility billing office A balance the provider claims is due That the patient paid it


Itemized statement Provider or facility billing office Line-level services and charges That each service was necessary


Explanation of Benefits Health plan How the plan processed a claim A demand for payment


## Who Reviews These, and Why the File Matters


Medical bills support claims well outside health insurance: bodily injury files for adjusters and SIU teams, hardship requests for lenders, and leave and reimbursement claims for employers.


The enforcement record is large and mostly concerns providers. The[Justice Department's June 2026 announcement](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/national-health-care-fraud-takedown-results-455-defendants-charged-connection-over-65) covered 455 defendants, and those are allegations. Provider-side schemes such as phantom billing and upcoding differ from a claimant editing a PDF, though both reach a reviewer as paper that looks routine.


NICB's Medical Fraud Scheme Guide describes template billing, where nearly identical data appears for many patients. NICB also warns in its AI guidance that generated supporting documents are simple to create, which lowers the skill needed to file a false claim.


## Edited Versus Generated


Edited-after-creation starts from a real provider document. The dates, the patient's name, the charges, or the balance change, while the letterhead, the account structure, and the provider's identifiers stay genuine. Those identifiers will pass a lookup, so the useful questions concern the numbers and the file's history.


Generated-from-scratch has no provider system behind it. The page can look complete, and its lines can reconcile, because they were composed together. The provider's billing office will have no matching account, which makes confirmation the decisive test for this class. The case note should name the suspected class. The wider difference between[verifying a document and examining it for fraud](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/document-verification-vs-document-fraud-detection) applies throughout.


## Checks a Reviewer Can Run Today


### NPI lookup in NPPES


When a bill prints a National Provider Identifier, look it up. The[NPI Registry](https://npiregistry.cms.hhs.gov/) is a free CMS directory of active NPI records, each a unique 10-digit number, and it publishes the provider's name, specialty, and practice address. Individuals and organizations hold separate records, so a bill showing a group's NPI alongside a physician's name can be correct.


The lookup catches numbers that do not exist, names that do not match, and specialties that do not fit the care billed. The registry states that issuing an NPI does not validate that a provider is licensed or credentialed, so licensure belongs to the state board. The registry is also public, which means a fake can carry a real provider's number.


### CMS code sets as a consistency check


[CMS's HCPCS page](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/healthcare-common-procedure-system) sets out the structure: Level I is CPT, maintained by the American Medical Association, using five numeric digits, and Level II, maintained by CMS, uses one letter followed by four digits for items such as ambulance services and durable medical equipment. Diagnoses use ICD-10-CM, which is updated on a published schedule.


Ask whether each code has the right form, existed on the date of service, matches its description, and plausibly relates to the diagnosis. CMS's National Correct Coding Initiative publishes procedure-to-procedure and medically unlikely edits that show code pairs and unit counts Medicare treats as problematic. Those edits are built for Medicare claims and a commercial payer may differ, so a conflict is a question for the provider. Clean codes prove nothing about a visit, since real codes can be copied.


### Reconcile the bill and the EOB


CMS tells patients to compare the bill to the EOB, including the amount owed. A reviewer can do the same, along with the arithmetic: total charges, adjustments, insurance payment, and patient payment should arrive at the balance. A bill for an insured patient with no matching EOB deserves a question. The absence is not conclusive, because some patients are self-pay and some claims were never filed. A statement date before the date of service needs an explanation.


### Read the file itself


Six classes of signal test the file's story. Production method asks whether the file came from a billing system, a later edit, or a generative pipeline. Timestamp trail compares[the file's creation and modification history](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/pdf-metadata-analysis-fraud-detection) against the statement date. Issuer matching asks whether the page fits the provider it names. Consistency compares totals, dates, and type across the page. Model artifacts are traces that generation leaves behind. Recycled patterns are the same layout, charges, or narrative across unrelated claimants, the machine-scale version of the template billing NICB describes. Portal downloads and office scans add noise, so one anomaly is a reason to look further.


## Confirming with the Provider


No analysis of a file proves that care was delivered. A clean forensic read can sit on top of an invented visit. The provider's own record does that job.


Find the billing office independently: the provider's published website, a health plan directory, or the NPPES practice address cross-checked against another source. Never use a phone number, email, or portal link printed on the document under review. Ask whether the account exists, whether the patient was seen on those dates, and whether the charges and balance match. Expect the office to require the patient's written authorization, and collect one with the claim file where the process allows it. For insured care, the plan's claim history is a second source.


Employers have additional limits. For FMLA medical certifications, 29 CFR 825.307 allows contact with the provider for authentication and clarification only by a health care provider, HR professional, leave administrator, or management official, and never the employee's direct supervisor.


## What to Do with a Suspect File


Hold the claim and request the itemized statement. Run the NPI lookup, the code checks, and the reconciliation. Confirm with the provider. Record whether the concern is an edit or a generated file, and route confirmed cases to the SIU, HR, or the fraud team under existing procedure. Lenders can apply the same order within[their wider document review](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/loan-document-fraud-detection) .


Before uploading a medical file to any tool, check how that tool handles protected health information. HHS treats health plans, clearinghouses, and providers that transmit electronic transactions as covered entities, and a vendor handling PHI on their behalf generally needs a business associate agreement. Ask each vendor about storage, retention, access, and model training, and have counsel confirm which rules apply. Once that review is done,[check the file](https://sphinxhq.com/products/doc-fraud) for a scored read of its history. The provider's answer remains the outside check.


### If you received a bill you do not recognize


Consumers should avoid paying from the contact details on a suspicious bill. Compare it to the EOB and call the provider or health plan using a number from an independent source, such as the insurance card. HHS-OIG advises contacting the provider first about questionable charges, then 1-800-MEDICARE for people on Medicare. Suspected Medicare fraud goes to the HHS-OIG hotline at 1-800-HHS-TIPS. Debt collection problems go to the CFPB, and scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### How can you tell if a medical bill is fake?


Check who issued it, look up any NPI in the NPPES registry, test the codes for form and consistency, and reconcile the balance with the EOB. Then confirm the account with the provider's billing office using contact details found independently.


### Is an Explanation of Benefits the same as a medical bill?


No. An EOB comes from the health plan and shows how a claim was processed, including what the plan will pay and what the patient may owe. CMS states that it is not a bill, and that the bill comes separately from the provider or facility.


### Does a valid NPI prove a medical bill is real?


No. NPIs are published in a free public registry, so a fake bill can carry a real provider's number. The registry also states that issuing an NPI does not validate a provider's license or credentials. A match shows the provider exists, and the billing office has to confirm the account.


### Is it safe to upload a medical bill to a document fraud tool?


Check first. A medical bill can contain protected health information, so confirm how the tool stores, retains, and accesses files, whether files train models, and whether a business associate agreement is needed for the organization's role.
